mcqs.question: What makes real-time scheduling's goal fundamentally different from the goals in the rest of this group (FCFS, SJF, Round Robin)?
options: Real-time scheduling only applies to systems with a single CPU core
Real-time scheduling doesn't use a ready queue at all
It requires every task to always meet its deadline — a near-miss is treated as a failure, not merely a worse average
It optimizes exclusively for total throughput, more aggressively than SJF
mcqs.explanation: The defining shift is from average-case optimization to a binary correctness requirement — meeting every deadline, every time, where missing even once counts as failure rather than a slightly worse metric. It isn't restricted to single-core systems, still uses queues conceptually, and isn't a throughput-maximization goal at all.

mcqs.question: A video conferencing app occasionally drops a frame under heavy load but keeps working acceptably. What category of real-time system is this?
options: Hard real-time, since it has timing requirements at all
Not a real-time system, since any timing requirement disqualifies it
Hard real-time, since audio/video always requires provable worst-case guarantees
Soft real-time — an occasional missed deadline degrades quality but isn't total failure
mcqs.explanation: Tolerating occasional missed deadlines as degraded-but-functional is exactly the soft real-time definition. Having timing requirements alone doesn't make something hard real-time — the consequence of a miss is what determines the category, and this system explicitly tolerates misses.

mcqs.question: A task set of two periodic tasks has total utilization U = 0.55. What does this tell you?
options: It's guaranteed unschedulable under any real-time algorithm
It's schedulable under EDF (U ≤ 1.0) and, since it's also under the RM bound for n=2 (~0.828), guaranteed schedulable under RM too
It's schedulable only if the CPU has at least two cores
Utilization values below 1.0 are meaningless for scheduling analysis
mcqs.explanation: U = 0.55 sits comfortably under both EDF's 1.0 exact bound and RM's more conservative ~0.828 bound for two tasks, so both algorithms can guarantee this task set meets its deadlines. It isn't unschedulable, isn't a multi-core-only result (this analysis is single-core), and utilization well under 1.0 is exactly the useful, meaningful case.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't simply raising a task's priority to maximum on a general-purpose OS give it real hard-real-time guarantees?
options: The kernel itself can still delay the task inside non-preemptible sections or drivers, and there's no formal schedulability analysis or bounded worst-case latency anywhere in the system
General-purpose kernels don't support priority levels at all
Priority levels only affect memory allocation, not CPU scheduling
Raising priority always causes an immediate kernel panic
mcqs.explanation: Priority only affects relative ordering among ready tasks — it says nothing about worst-case delay from kernel-internal non-preemptible sections, interrupt handling, or drivers, none of which a plain priority bump touches. General-purpose kernels do support priority levels, priority isn't a memory-allocation mechanism, and it doesn't cause a panic.

mcqs.question: A high-priority task is blocked on a lock held by a low-priority task, and an unrelated medium-priority task keeps preempting the low-priority one. What is this called, and what fixes it?
options: Deadlock; fixed by killing the medium-priority task
Starvation; fixed by adding more CPU cores
The convoy effect; fixed by switching to Round Robin
Priority inversion; fixed by priority inheritance, temporarily boosting the lock-holder to the waiting task's priority
mcqs.explanation: This is the textbook priority inversion pattern (famously seen on Mars Pathfinder), fixed by priority inheritance so the lock-holder can't be indefinitely delayed by an unrelated medium-priority task. It's not deadlock (no circular wait), not the convoy effect, and not resolved by more cores or killing the medium task.

mcqs.question: A task's deadline is shorter than its period (it must finish well before it's due to run again). Which fixed-priority algorithm correctly handles this, unlike plain Rate Monotonic?
options: Deadline Monotonic, which prioritizes by relative deadline instead of period
First-Come-First-Served, since arrival order accounts for any deadline
Plain Rate Monotonic handles this case correctly with no changes needed
Round Robin, since equal time slices make deadline irrelevant
mcqs.explanation: Deadline Monotonic generalizes RM by prioritizing on relative deadline rather than period, correctly handling the case where they differ — plain RM's period-based priority can misorder tasks when deadline and period diverge. FCFS and Round Robin have no deadline-awareness at all.
